edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. VI, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 28)

source_text: Si quis dicat: alius est qui passus est, et alius, qui non est passus; et non confitetur, idem impassibile et immutabile Dei Verbum, in carne propria passum immutabiliter, sicut scriptum est; anathema esto. Qua ratione dici potest alius qui passus est, et alius, qui non est passus? cum ipse Dominus dicat: Oportet filium hominis multa pati, et occidi; et die tertia resurgere a mortuis. Et illud: cum videritis filium hominis sedentem in dextera patris, et: cum venerit filius hominis in gloria patris sui.
thought_title: The Word who cannot suffer suffered in his own flesh
orientation: Gregory condemns making the one who suffered someone other than the one who cannot suffer: the same Word suffered in his own flesh without change.
pass_a_gloss: If anyone says: one (alius) is he who suffered (passus est), and another (alius) who did not suffer; and does not confess the same (idem) impassible (impassibile) and immutable (immutabile) Word of God (Dei Verbum) [to have] suffered in his own flesh (carne propria) immutably (immutabiliter), as it is written; let him be anathema. By what reason can it be said [that] one is he who suffered, and another who did not suffer? when the Lord himself says: It is necessary (oportet) [for] the son of man to suffer many things, and be killed (occidi); and on the third day rise again (resurgere) from the dead. And that: when you see the son of man sitting (sedentem) at the right hand (dextera) of the father, and: when the son of man comes in the glory (gloria) of his father.

pass_b_english: If anyone says, “The one who suffered is someone other than the one who did not suffer,” and does not confess that the same Word of God, impassible and unchangeable, suffered in his own flesh without change, as it is written, let him be anathema.

How can it be said that the one who suffered is someone other than the one who did not suffer, when the Lord himself says, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be killed, and on the third day rise from the dead” (Luke 9:22); and this, “When you see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Father” (Mark 14:62); and, “When the Son of Man comes in the glory of his Father” (Mark 8:38)?
notes: Impassibile kept as the doctrinal term “impassible”; immutabiliter rendered “without change”.
The first saying matches Luke 9:22 (die tertia; Mark 8:31 has “after three days”; Matthew 16:21 is parallel).
The second saying is closest to Mark 14:62 / Matthew 26:64, which read “at the right hand of Power”; this text has “of the Father”, and the reading is translated as it stands.
The third saying matches Mark 8:38 (cum venerit … in gloria Patris sui), with parallels Matthew 16:27 and Luke 9:26.
Margin sigla Marc. 8, Luc. 9, Mat. 16, Marc. 8, Luc. 9; the facing Greek margin has al. anathematizestho (no change of sense).
“As it is written” in the anathema has no single target and is left uncited.
